item.title: Police say the 24-year-old who fatally shot 6 people in a Krakow square has died in the hospital
item.description:
Police say the 24-year-old who fatally shot 6 people in a Krakow square has died in the hospital
Police said the 24-year-old who opened fire in a city square in Poland, killing six people and wounding 15 on Saturday, died in the hospital Monday morningByThe Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 1:33 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KRAKOW, Poland -- The 24-year-old who opened fire in a city square in Poland, killing six people and wounding 15 on Saturday, died in the hospital Monday morning, police said.
The man had been in critical condition after police shot him to end the attack and had had several operations.
The assailant drove through the square in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town on Saturday to start the attack. The square is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.

item.title: He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon's presidential bid may hand it power
item.description:
He fought France's far right for half a century. Now Mélenchon's presidential bid may hand it power
Jean-Luc Mélenchon is 75 and he's betting his last shot at France’s presidency on a generation young enough to be his grandchildrenByTHOMAS ADAMSON Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 12:03 AM
Share
LE BOURGET, France -- Young supporters wore his name on their backs like a soccer star’s, above the number 27. They sang about brass bands and revolution. Many had spent the fall protesting or blockading their schools.
Then in walked Jean-Luc Mélenchon: 75 years old, on his fourth presidential run and old enough to be their grandfather.
“I have only one sensible thing to propose,” he told 20,000 supporters in a vast hall north of Paris on Saturday. “Everything must change.”
The septuagenarian may never get another chance. Three presidential bids have ended short of the runoff. In 2022, just 421,308 votes kept him out. Now, riding a surge in support, he is eyeing a winner-take-all showdown with far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen.
The bespectacled, booming and seemingly tireless leftist wants more than the presidency. He wants to rewrite the rules of the French republic — invoking the unfinished promise of the Revolution of 1789.
A place in the May 2 runoff could prove a cruel prize. If Le Pen beats him, the anti-capitalist who has spent half a century fighting the far right could help give it what it has never won: the Elysee Palace — and command of France’s nuclear arsenal.
Victory could send shock waves across the Atlantic. Trump would still be in the White House. Russia is waging war in Ukraine. Yet Mélenchon wants to pull the EU’s only nuclear-armed power out of NATO, starting with its military command. His debt plans could also put France on a collision course with Europe’s central bank, rattling markets.

item.title: Death toll rises to 39 after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal
item.description:
Death toll rises to 39 after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal
The death toll in Senegal’s boat capsize has risen to 39 after new bodies were discovered Monday, according to the country’s emergency servicesByBABAKAR DIONE Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 6:40 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
DAKAR, Senegal -- The death toll from the capsize off Senegal of a boat carrying migrants rose to 39 following the discovery of more bodies on Monday, the country’s emergency services said.
The boat, which left Saint-Louis in northern Senegal and was headed to the Spanish coast, overturned on Sunday, offshore from the town of Kébémer, north of the capital Dakar.
The Ministry of Interior said Sunday at least 21 people had died and rescuers were looking for possible survivors. It did not say how many people were on the boat, but several passengers are still believed to be missing.
Only one passenger was rescued alive.

The boat was following a well-traveled migration route for thousands of young Senegalese seeking better economic conditions. They travel on uncovered wooden canoes for around 800 miles on the Atlantic Ocean to reach Europe. Young people face high unemployment and poverty as the country struggles with an economic crisis.
Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye offered condolences and vowed to clamp down on networks behind the dangerous crossings.

item.title: US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
item.description:
US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing its five-year markByThe Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 12:01 AM
Share
For the first time since February, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. negotiators are scheduled to hold talks on ending the full-scale war that is nearing the five-year mark, with security guarantees topping the agenda.
The two-day session starting Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, follows previous negotiations early this year that failed to produce any visible progress toward ending Europe’s most devastating conflict since World War II.
The talks follow last month's localized truce around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine that was brokered with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump and allowed the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of desperately needed humanitarian supplies.
But even as Moscow and Kyiv touted the weeklong ceasefire as a positive model, fierce fighting has continued along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line. Both sides also have escalated their long-range attacks on each other with drones and missiles.
Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukraine’s power system, seeking to undermine the country’s resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and new, faster jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
A look at the talks and what's on the agenda:
Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on key elements of any prospective peace deal.

item.title: Japan to provide coastal radar and drones to the Philippines under $27M deal
item.description:
Japan to provide coastal radar and drones to the Philippines under $27M deal
Japan said it will provide a coastal radar system and unmanned aircraft to the Philippines under a security aid deal, as both countries face growing tensions with ChinaByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 10:09 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan said it will provide a coastal surveillance radar system and unmanned aircraft to the Philippines under a security deal signed Monday, as the two defense partners face growing tensions with China.
Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Katsuro Kitagawa and Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro signed the 4.3 billion yen ($27 million) deal at a ceremony in Manila, Japan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The radar system will go to the Philippine Navy and the uncrewed aerial vehicles to the Philippine Air Force. The equipment is intended to strengthen maritime security and surveillance in the strategically important country, which sits near key sea lanes, the ministry said.
The deal marks the first transfer of finished Japanese-made defense equipment through Japan’s Official Security Assistance program. Established in 2023 as a military counterpart to its official development assistance program, OSA aims to help developing nations address challenges posed by China’s growing influence.
Japan has been accelerating its military and arms industry buildup. It lifted a ban on lethal weapons exports earlier this year and has agreed with the Philippines to begin talks on a deal that would allow Tokyo to provide used destroyers to Manila’s navy.
Separately on Monday, the leaders of Japan and Vietnam held talks in Tokyo and pledged to deepen cooperation in defense, energy and economic security amid China’s growing regional influence.

item.title: Overnight strikes in Yemen kill at least 1 person and wound 9, and other Mideast news
item.description:
Overnight strikes in Yemen kill at least 1 person and wound 9, and other Mideast news
Overnight strikes in Yemen have hit a gas station and an oil facility, killing at least one person and wounding nine othersByThe Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 7:06 AM
Share
Overnight strikes hit a gas station and an oil facility in Yemen, killing at least one person and wounding nine, residents and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels said on Tuesday.
In Iran, a top security official claimed that the Iran war had already “wrecked” the United States, and called on Washington to accept seven demands that Tehran has made for an end to the conflict.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Read our full coverage here.
Houthi-run health ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said in a statement on X on Tuesday that a strike hit a gas station in a district of Yemen's capital, Sanaa, killing one person and wounding three others.
He said another airstrike targeted an oil company, wounding at least six people, causing “extensive damage” to nearby homes and shops and panicking residents.
Al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia for both strikes. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify his claims.
The strikes come amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces that escalated this summer. The rebels continue to target Saudi energy facilities and airports as part of a campaign they say is meant to push Saudi Arabia into lifting its blockade on Yemen.
Sanaa resident Khaled al-Khawlani told the AP on Tuesday that he was horrified by the explosions that targeted the oil facility near residential areas of Sanaa at around 4 a.m.
Another resident said the explosions shattered his windows and reverberated across the city while people slept. The resident spoke on condition of anonymity for security reasons.

item.title: Honduran court delays verdict in disappearance case that exposed sex trafficking ring
item.description:
Honduran court delays verdict in disappearance case that exposed sex trafficking ring
A Honduran court has postponed a verdict in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie PeñaByANNA-CATHERINE BRIGIDA Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 2:28 PM
MEXICO CITY -- A Honduran court postponed a verdict Monday in a sex-trafficking case linked to the 2022 disappearance of Angie Peña, delaying a decision until Nov. 20 as relatives, lawyers and women's rights groups demanded justice.
The case has drawn attention to allegations of impunity and corruption that advocates say have allowed widespread gender violence in the Central American country.
Four men are on trial for crimes related to Peña’s disappearance. Two U.S. citizens, Harold Green and William James Murdock, face human trafficking charges, while another U.S. citizen, Gary Lee Johnston, and Honduran Gustavo Trejo are accused of criminal association.
The case has implicated public officials and exposed a criminal ring known as “Delta Teams” that has drawn comparison to the Jeffrey Epstein network in a country with high rates of gender violence and low conviction rates for related crimes.
Lawyers representing the family have questioned the lack of transparency of the investigation and trial, which was not open to the press or general public. Peña's family said it has received death threats, and the August killing of Dereck McNeil, a key protected witness, further exposed the dangers of seeking justice in Honduras.
“There are many more women and girls who have been victims of trafficking networks, and those cases are silenced, they go unpunished,” said Kenia Paz, a lawyer for the Legal Team for Human Rights who represents Peña's family.
She said the case has exposed a criminal network “beyond what we can even imagine” and called for the state to provide answers on what happened to Peña.

item.title: Pope draws 2.5M to Mass in Argentina, says people with disabilities are a blessing
item.description:
Pope draws 2.5M to Mass in Argentina, says people with disabilities are a blessing
Pope Leo XIV has drawn 2.5 million people to his first Mass in ArgentinaByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, ALMUDENA CALATRAVA Associated Press, DEBORA REY Associated Press, and ISABEL DEBRE Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 7:29 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Pope Leo XIV visited a home for people with disabilities Monday and told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden, as he pressed his call for Argentina to care for its most vulnerable in a symbolic rebuke of President Javier Milei’s austerity measures.
Before drawing an estimated 2.5 million people to his first Mass in Argentina, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires. Founded by an Italian priest in 1935, the institution houses more than 400 people with disabilities on its 123-acre (50-hectare) grounds.
The center, known as the “city of charity,” has been hit hard by Milei’s austerity measures, which have severely affected healthcare and social services. Milei has taken his signature chain saw to specialized therapy programs that for decades have been a lifeline for many of Argentina’s estimated 5 million people with disabilities, freezing payments and dismantling a vital safety net.
Some residents and employees wept as Leo arrived Monday and embraced people in wheelchairs. He told them their lives were a blessing, not a burden on society.
“You can help us to remember the foundation of the dignity of every human being and what is truly important in life,” Leo said in the center’s chapel.
“A nation’s progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs,” he added.

item.title: In Senegal, Black surfers want to reclaim the waves despite lack of resources
item.description:
In Senegal, Black surfers want to reclaim the waves despite lack of resources
The origins of surfing can be traced back to the native populations of Peru, Polynesia and Hawaii, and European travelers documented children surfing along the coast of what is now Ghana as early as the 17th centuryByMONIKA PRONCZUK Associated PressNovember 9, 2026, 5:28 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
DAKAR, Senegal -- Ibra Samb first saw people carrying surfboards when he was a little boy, studying at a Quran school in a fishing village in Senegal. Together with friends, he hid from teachers and parents and followed the surfers — who were all white foreigners — to the beach.
“They were gliding over the waves,” said the 28-year-old professional surfer. “To us, it was incredible. Seeing them stand up on their boards, we just wanted to try it ourselves.”
Samb and his friends could not afford surfboards, so they used pieces of plywood they found on the beach, leftovers from colorful pirogue fishing boats. Little did he know that surfing would eventually bring him opportunities to compete around the world, access to international sponsorships and a sense of belonging and purpose.
As the world watches Senegal host the Youth Olympic Games this month — the first Olympic event ever held in Africa — Senegalese surfers hope they can get more resources and visibility on the global surf scene to be able to fulfill their potential.
The origins of surfing can be traced back to the native populations of Peru, Polynesia and Hawaii. But today's surfing, especially professional surfing, is predominantly white.
In West Africa, only a fortunate few can afford expensive equipment and training. A used beginner's surfboard costs around $200, which is double the country's monthly minimum wage.
For professionals, visas are hard to obtain and traveling is costly. Despite Africa's extraordinary coastline, African surfers remain rare at the highest level of competitive surfing.

item.title: Indonesia's vice president offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
item.description:
Indonesia's vice president offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
Indonesia’s Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has offered to resign amid mounting pressure over his academic credentials, officials sayByNINIEK KARMINI Associated Press and EDNA TARIGAN Associated PressNovember 10, 2026, 7:00 AM
Share
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.
It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to “continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents,” Hadi said.
As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.
“I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place,” Raka said. “I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy.”
The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.
Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.
